title: Architecturing metallic materials via severe plastic deformation: from microstructural refinement to mesoscale design
abstract: Abstract For the past three decades, severe plastic deformation (SPD) has been established as a paramount top–down strategy for producing ultrafine-grained (UFG) materials with exceptional strength. However, efforts to produce fully homogeneous microstructures inevitably run up against the fundamental limitations imposed by the opposing requirements of strength and ductility. This article highlights a paradigm shift in this field: the evolution from simple micro- or nanostructuring to deformation-enabled architecturing. We propose reframing SPD not simply as a means of grain refinement, but as a platform for generating tailored strain fields—vortical, spiral, graded, and beyond—that enable the mesoscale synthesis of architectured materials. Here, we systematically classify deformation-induced architectures into harmonic, layered, and hybrid/composite systems. We discuss how specific processing routes, including twist extrusion and co-deformation, can serve as lithography-free methods to create complex internal geometries and heterogeneous microstructures simultaneously. A critical focus is placed on the synergistic strengthening mechanisms arising from this engineered heterogeneity, specifically hetero-deformation-induced (HDI) hardening, back-stress generation, and strain partitioning between soft and hard domains. Finally, we outline the roadmap for translating these laboratory-scale concepts into industrial applications, addressing the challenges of scale-up, interface integrity, and design for manufacturing. This perspective offers a unified framework for designing the next generation of advanced metallic materials that defy conventional property limits.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Achieving high strength without sacrificing ductility has long been one of the most persistent challenges in structural metallic materials. Over the past three decades, severe plastic deformation (SPD) came to the fore as the most potent top–down strategy to address this dilemma. Pioneering works by Segal, Valiev, Langdon, and others demonstrated that processing metals through techniques such as equal-channel angular pressing (ECAP) [ 1 ,  2 ] and high-pressure torsion (HPT) [ 3 ,  4 ] can refine grain sizes to the submicron or nanometer scale [ 5 ,  6 ], achieving exceptional strength improvements without the addition of alloying elements. The development of such ultrafine-grained (UFG) materials using a plethora of SPD techniques [ 7 ,  8 – 9 ] opened new horizons in materials science, where realizing a homogeneous submicron- and nanostructure was traditionally considered the gold standard for maximizing performance.

This article highlights a shift in perspective: SPD processes are no longer viewed solely as grain refinement tools into powerful platforms for manufacturing such architectured materials. We define this emerging paradigm as  deformation-enabled architecturing . While the traditional perspective viewed SPD merely as a forming process for shaping, the new paradigm reinterprets SPD as a “field generator” [ 18 ]. Processes like twist extrusion (TE) [ 19 ,  20 ] or the cone–cone method [ 21 ] can impose complex topologies of the strain field within the material, such as spiral, vortex, or gradient flows. This enables the mechanical hybridization of dissimilar metals or the spatial control of microstructural distribution within a single material, thereby realizing heterogeneous structures in one processing step. The outline of this article, with its focus on the transition in SPD research from nanostructuring to architecturing, is as follows. First, Sect. 2 addresses the design principles and classification of architectured metals (layered, harmonic, hybrid, etc. [ 22 ]). Section 3  introduces key SPD processing technologies (twist extrusion, co-deformation, etc.) for realizing these structures. Section 4 provides an in-depth discussion of the strengthening mechanisms generated by structural heterogeneity, specifically hetero-deformation-induced (HDI) hardening and back stress [ 23 ,  24 – 25 ]. Finally, we present strategies for scaling up from laboratory-scale research to industrial applications and offer an outlook for the future.

sections.heading: Reducing the “holes” in material property space
paragraphs: The traditional development of structural materials has primarily relied on chemical alloying and microstructural refinement by plastic deformation and heat treatment to improve mechanical properties. While successful, these approaches are bounded by intrinsic physical limits, often represented as the “banana curve” or trade-off relationship between strength and ductility. As conceptualized by Ashby, when material properties are mapped onto property charts (e.g., strength vs. density, stiffness vs. damping), vast regions remain unpopulated—referred to as “holes” in the material property space [ 11 ,  12 ].

Reducing these holes requires a departure from uniform monolithic designs toward “hybrid” or “architectured” materials. By combining two or more materials (or phases) with distinct properties, hybrids can achieve performance characteristics that lie beyond a simple rule of mixtures. For instance, placing a hard phase at the surface of a material for wear resistance while maintaining a tough core for damage tolerance allows for multifunctionality that a single homogeneous material cannot offer. In this context, the design strategy shifts from  processing for homogeneity  to  processing for controlled heterogeneity . The innovative potential of microstructure engineering focusing on the creation of heterogeneous structures has been highlighted in a recent focus issue of  Nature Materials  [ 26 ]. The approach we wish to promulgate through this article is in line with this emerging alloy design paradigm. The specificity of SPD-based architecturing and its greatest advantage are that it enables a double benefit: architecturing at mesoscale combined with strengthening by extreme microstructure refinement, which is a forte of SPD processing.

Figure  1  illustrates the proposed fundamental paradigm shift in materials design. As depicted in Fig.  1 , conventional homogeneous materials occupy restricted regions within the material property space (e.g., strength versus ductility represented by uniform elongation), leaving vast “holes” that remain inaccessible through traditional alloying or simple grain refinement. To access these uncharted domains, a strategic transition is required: moving away from the “First Generation” pursuit of homogeneous ultrafine-grained structures toward the “Second Generation” design of heterogeneous architectures, as shown in Fig.  1 . By deliberately introducing mesoscale heterogeneity through harmonic cores, laminate arrangements, or gradient structures [ 22 ], architectured materials can activate synergistic strengthening mechanisms that are unavailable to their uniform counterparts, thereby effectively narrowing the gaps in the property charts. Figure 1 A conceptual strength–elongation map illustrating the well-known “hole” in the strength–ductility domain and its mitigation via mesoscale architecturing. The left panel depicts the traditional trade-off for homogeneous coarse, fine, and ultrafine-grained materials, delineating a property regime unattainable through grain refinement alone. The right panel shows that mesoscale architectures can contract this inaccessible region by promoting heterostructured deformation modes, with representative motifs (layered, harmonic, gradient) indicated schematically. The figure is qualitative and not to scale; its purpose is to emphasize that architecturing can diminish—but not fully close—the gap.

To date, the majority of SPD-driven architecturing studies have been conducted on metallic materials. SPD techniques are particularly advantageous for the fabrication of metallic nanocomposites, as evidenced by research on nanocomposite generation, accumulative roll-bonded Al–SiC composites, and HPT-processed metal hybrids [ 27 ,  28 – 29 ]. In addition, SPD processing has also been successfully applied to tailor the microstructure, internal architecture, and both mechanical and physical properties of polymers [ 30 ]. Notably, in many systems the property-modifying effects of SPD are even more pronounced in polymers than in metals.

sections.heading: Defining architecture at mesoscale
paragraphs: A “microstructure” encompasses features from the atomic to the micrometer scales, including point defects, dislocations, precipitates, and grains, while “macrostructure” describes the dimensions and geometry of the structural component itself. “Architecture” is defined at the mesoscale, representing an intermediate regime that links intrinsic material features to the behavior of the structural member [ 14 ,  22 ,  31 ,  32 ].

In the context of metallic materials, architecture is characterized by three key descriptors: Geometry : The specific spatial arrangement of constituent phases (e.g., layered, fibrous, cellular, or gradient). Length Scale : The characteristic size of the architectural features, which is typically larger than the grain size but smaller than the component dimensions (grain < architecture < sample). Interface : The nature of the boundaries separating the domains (e.g., discrete bonded interfaces in laminates or gradient interphases in harmonic structures).

A central message of this paper is that severe plastic deformation offers a distinctive platform for shaping mesoscale architectures. In contrast to additive manufacturing or bonding approaches, SPD generates architecture through deformation‑driven mixing and controlled strain topologies, while preserving integral metallic bonding and crystallographic continuity across interfaces [ 18 ].

The proposed strategy is broadly applicable to ductile metallic systems, yet its effectiveness is not universal. The best candidates typically share (i) sufficient intrinsic plasticity in at least one domain to accommodate strain without early cracking, (ii) adequate strain-hardening capacity, (iii) controllable domain contrast and architectural length scale to sustain incompatibility over a significant strain range, and (iv) robust interfaces that preserve constraint under large strain (where relevant, cyclic loading). In contrast, systems dominated by brittle constituents, unstable interfaces (e.g., debonding or rapid intermetallic formation), or insufficient hardening capacity may show limited benefits or premature failure despite high strength.

sections.heading: Classification of deformation-enabled architectures
paragraphs: To systematically understand the potential of SPD-based architecturing [ 33 ], we classify the architectures into four distinct motifs based on their topological characteristics (Fig.  2 ): Figure 2 Classification of mesoscale architecture motifs produced by deformation processing.  a  Harmonic structure exhibiting a coarse-grained core surrounded by a contiguous ultrafine-grained network shell [ 24 ].  b  Layered architecture consisting of alternating domains with different hardness, typically produced by ARB [ 35 ] and cone–cone processing [ 36 ].  c  Vortex-like chiral flow pattern generated within a square cross-section by twist extrusion [ 20 ].  d  3 D  spiral fiber architecture embedded in a metal matrix, produced by co-deformation [ 40 ].

sections.heading: Harmonic and network structures
paragraphs: Proposed by Ameyama et al. [ 34 ], the harmonic structure represents a bimodal architecture where three-dimensional, continuously connected network of ultrafine-grained (UFG) “shells” enclose coarse-grained (CG) “cores” [ 24 ]. This topological design mimics natural cellular materials, allowing the hard shell to carry high loads while the soft core accommodates plastic strain, thereby delaying strain localization and failure.

sections.heading: Layered and laminate structures
paragraphs: These are composed of alternating layers of dissimilar metals (e.g., Al/Cu, steel/Ni) or same-metal layers with different grain sizes. SPD processes such as accumulative roll bonding (ARB) [ 35 ] are archetypal methods for creating such architectures. The key design parameters here are the layer thickness and the interface density, which govern the transition from pile-up dominated hardening to confined plasticity [ 36 ].

sections.heading: Gradient structures
paragraphs: Gradient architectures exhibit a gradual variation in microstructure (e.g., grain size or dislocation density) from the surface to the interior. Surface mechanical attrition treatment (SMAT) [ 37 ,  38 ] and torsional deformation naturally create such gradients, where the surface is hardened enhancing fatigue resistance while the core remains ductile.

sections.heading: Vortex, chiral, and spiral structures
paragraphs: A more complex class of architectures arises from rotational deformation paths, such as those involved in twist extrusion or high-pressure torsion of assembled preforms. These processes induce vortex-like flow, creating chiral or spiral patterns of the constituent materials [ 19 ,  20 ,  39 ,  40 ]. These 3 D  architectures are particularly promising for inducing multiple crack deflections, thus enhancing torsional toughness by offering energy dissipation channels unavailable in simple 2 D  laminates.

sections.heading: Processing: SPD as a field generator for architecturing
paragraphs: Traditional metal forming processes focus on changing the  external shape  of a workpiece. By contrast, deformation-enabled architecturing utilizes SPD processes to manipulate the  internal structure  while maintaining (or cyclically restoring) the external geometry. To achieve this, the processing tool must act as a “field generator,” capable of imparting spatially programmable strain topologies within the material, such as shear, rotation, and compression [ 18 ]. This section categorizes key SPD routes based on their capability to generate specific architectural motifs.

Specifically, Fig.  3  summarizes how the key SPD processes discussed in this article generate programmable strain fields within the material. As illustrated in Fig.  3 a, twist extrusion [ 19 ,  20 ] imposes a rotational vortex flow field within the transverse cross-section of the billet, enabling the synthesis of chiral architectures. The cone–cone method [ 21 ], shown in Fig.  3 b, applies a continuous severe shear strain field through the sheet thickness, effectively controlling layered structures. Furthermore, the co-deformation strategy via torsion, depicted in Fig.  3 c, functions as a geometric mapping tool that transforms linear reinforcements into 3D spiral topologies. These capabilities of SPD as a “field generator” serve as the fundamental basis for manufacturing architectured metals. Figure 3 Representative SPD processes acting as strain field generators for architecturing.  a  Twist extrusion imposing a rotational shear flow field that induces vortex-like mixing [ 20 ].  b  The cone–cone method applying continuous severe shear to sheet materials for layered architecturing [ 21 ].  c  Torsional co-deformation transforming linear fibers into spiral/helical topologies through geometric constraint [ 40 ].

sections.heading: Twist extrusion (TE): vortex flow and chiral architecture
paragraphs: Twist extrusion is a powerful method for generating three‑dimensional architectures with rotational symmetry. In TE, a billet with a non‑circular cross‑section is extruded through a die whose channel twists along its axis—typically by a prescribed angle such as 60° or 90° [ 20 ]. This distinctive process geometry produces characteristic kinematic features and architecturing capabilities: Vortex‑like flow field : The kinematics of TE induce a vortex‑like material flow in the transverse plane. This motion is not a rigid‑body rotation but a severe mixing process in which material elements near the periphery follow longer trajectories than those near the center. Architecturing capability : When a multi‑material billet (e.g., a stacked or bundled preform) is fed into a TE die, the vortex flow stretches and folds the constituent phases, effectively synthesizing a hybrid material. Simple longitudinal fibers can be transformed into helical or chiral architectures embedded within a matrix, offering geometric freedom unattainable with conventional rolling or straight‑channel extrusion [ 18 ].

sections.heading: The cone–cone method (CCM): continuous layering and gradients
paragraphs: While twist extrusion is ideal for bulk billets, the cone–cone method, proposed by Bouaziz, Estrin, and Kim, offers a continuous processing route for sheet materials or hollow cylinders [ 21 ]. This method is characterized by the following operational principles and architectural features: Process principle : The material is fed between two rotating conical dies. The friction and compressive forces impose severe shear strain and high hydrostatic pressure throughout the thickness of the sheet. Architecturing capability : CCM is particularly effective for producing layered or laminated architectures. By feeding stacked sheets of dissimilar metals, CCM promotes solid-state bonding via massive shear deformation while refining the microstructure of each layer simultaneously. Furthermore, by controlling the rotation speed and friction conditions, gradient structures (where strain accumulation varies from the surface to the middle of the sheet) can be manufactured in a continuous process.

sections.heading: Co-deformation strategies: spiral and hybrid systems
paragraphs: The synthesis of hybrid architectures often requires the co-deformation of mechanically contrasting materials (e.g., hard wires in a soft matrix). Khoddam et al. demonstrated this using a torsion-based approach to fabricate spiral fiber-reinforced composites [ 40 ]. The realization of such hybrid systems relies on controlling two critical aspects: Strain compatibility : The principal difficulty in co‑deformation is avoiding damage and fracture of the harder phase. Achieving successful architecturing requires identifying a processing window in which the hydrostatic pressure inherent to SPD suppresses damage, enabling otherwise brittle reinforcements to undergo plastic co‑deformation with the ductile matrix. Geometric transformation : Torsional deformation transforms linear reinforcements into spiral/helical entities. This geometric transformation is crucial because spiral architectures effectively convert tensile loads into compressive stresses along the fibers, enhancing the overall toughness and damage tolerance of the resulting composite.

sections.heading: Mechanisms: synergistic strengthening in architectured metals
paragraphs: The defining characteristic of architectured metallic materials is that their mechanical performance exceeds the prediction of the linear rule of mixtures. This phenomenon results from the synergy of complex micromechanical interactions between the constituent domains (e.g., soft matrix in conjunction with hard reinforcement, or coarse-grained core combined with ultrafine-grained shell). In this section, we outline the governing mechanisms that underpin this synergy, with particular emphasis on how deformation‑enabled architectures enhance work hardening and improve damage tolerance.

sections.heading: Plastic strain gradient and load transfer
paragraphs: In a deformation-enabled architecture, the constituents typically possess distinct yield strengths. Upon loading, plastic deformation is initiated first in the mechanically softer domains (e.g., the coarse-grained core in a harmonic structure), while the harder domains (e.g., the UFG shell) remain elastic [ 24 ]. This plastic incompatibility gives rise to two critical micromechanical effects: Plastic strain gradient : This mismatch creates a mechanical constraint. The soft and hard domains are forced to co-deform, leading to significant load partitioning. The soft domains accommodate most of the plastic strain and thus provide ductility, while the hard domains carry most of the load, providing strength to the material [ 14 ]. Triaxiality : The geometric constraint imposed by the rigid architecture (e.g., a honeycomb-like UFG network) induces a complex triaxial stress state in the soft domains, which can suppress void nucleation and delay fracture.

sections.heading: Hetero-deformation-induced (HDI) hardening and back stress
paragraphs: Arguably the most critical contribution of architecturing to the strength-ductility balance is the generation of back stress. The mechanistic pathway for this strengthening involves three sequential stages: GND accumulation : Due to the load partitioning described above, distinct plastic strain gradients develop near the interfaces between soft and hard domains. To accommodate these gradients and maintain continuity of crystal lattice, geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs) pile up at the domain boundaries [ 41 ,  42 ]. Long-range internal stress : These piled-up GNDs generate a long-range internal stress field, known as back stress, which opposes the forward motion of dislocations in the soft phase. (An internal stress promoting plastic deformation in the hard phase emerges concurrently.) The occurrence of back stress acts as a kinematic hardening mechanism. Overall stress : The total flow stress is expressed as the sum of the “friction stress” (not associated with the stress field produced by dislocations) and the back stress.

To visualize the origin of this favorable interplay of soft and hard constituents of architectured metals, Fig.  4  schematically illustrates the HDI hardening mechanism operating therein. As shown in Fig.  4 a, the mechanical contrast between soft and hard domains induces drastic plastic strain incompatibility upon loading. As mentioned above, GNDs pile up at the interface as depicted in Fig.  4 b, generating a long-range back stress that opposes dislocation motion in the soft domains. Consequently, as revealed in the stress–strain curves in Fig.  4 c, the architectured material exhibits additional extra work hardening derived from this back stress, thereby suppressing early necking and achieving a superior strength-ductility combination compared to microstructurally homogeneous materials. Figure 4 Illustration of the synergistic strengthening mechanism in architectured metals.  a  Plastic strain contrast between soft (core) and hard (shell) domains due to mechanical contrast [ 24 ].  b  GNDs pile up at domain boundaries to absorb plastic strain mismatch, generating long-range back stress.  c  Back stress leads to extra work hardening (HDI hardening), delaying the onset of plastic instability thus enhancing ductility, while at the same time raising strength beyond the rule of mixtures. Figures from Ref. [ 24 ] are under the terms of CC-BY 4.0 license.

In conventional plasticity, the increase in flow stress with strain (work hardening, often termed strain hardening) can be viewed as the combined contribution of an isotropic component and a kinematic component. Isotropic hardening raises the overall resistance to plastic flow by increasing the average obstacle strength or stored dislocation density. In contrast, kinematic hardening represents a directional effect associated with long-range internal stresses that bias subsequent yielding, often manifested as a Bauschinger-like response upon load reversal. In heterogeneous architectures, kinematic hardening arises naturally because plastic incompatibility between soft and hard domains creates strain gradients that require GNDs to maintain compatibility. The resulting long-range internal stress field acts as back stress, which effectively translates the yield surface and contributes an additional hardening component beyond conventional isotropic hardening.

The macroscopic work-hardening rate can therefore be interpreted as the sum of (i) a friction/isotropic contribution and (ii) a back-stress (kinematic) contribution. In the context of metals architectured to generate a heterostructure, the term HDI hardening emphasizes that this additional hardening is activated by sustained heterogeneous deformation. Plastic incompatibility between domains continuously generates and maintains back stress in the soft domains during forward loading. A compact representation for the flow stress is  σ  =  σ f  +  σ b , where  σ f  is the isotropic component, often referred to as “friction stress,” and  σ b  is the back stress, or kinematic, component.

As demonstrated for harmonic structured materials, this HDI hardening produces an unusually high work-hardening rate, which effectively delays necking and results in superior tensile ductility while maintaining the high strength of the material [ 24 ,  43 ,  44 ]. This mechanism explains why deformation-enabled architectures often outperform homogeneous UFG materials, which lack such internal interface networks and the attendant non-uniformity of plastic strain.

sections.heading: Crack blunting and deflection via topology
paragraphs: Beyond yielding and work hardening, the topology of inner architecture plays a pivotal role in fracture mechanics. Depending on the specific architectural motif, the enhancement of fracture resistance is realized through two primary toughening mechanisms: Crack blunting : In layered or harmonic architectures, a crack initiating in a brittle/hard layer is often arrested or blunted when it encounters a boundary of a ductile/soft layer. The interface acts as a barrier, forcing the crack to re-nucleate or change its propagation direction. Crack deflection (Tortuosity) : In 3D architectures such as spiral or chiral structures produced by twist extrusion, the crack path is forced to follow a tortuous route along the helical interfaces [ 18 ]. This increases the total energy dissipation, thus inhibiting fracture. Khoddam et al. showed that spiral fiber architectures can effectively convert tensile failure modes into shear-dominated modes, significantly enhancing the total work of fracture compared to straight-fiber counterparts [ 40 ].

sections.heading: Concluding remarks: from uniformity to inner architecture
paragraphs: This article has articulated a transformative shift in the field of severe plastic deformation: the emerging transition from nanostructuring for homogeneous ultrafine-grained materials to deformation-enabled architecturing for heterogeneous systems. We have demonstrated that SPD processes, when viewed as “strain field generators,” offer a unique lithography-free platform to imprint complex mesoscale architectures into metallic materials, including harmonic networks and gradients to spiral/chiral hybrids. The core value of this approach lies not merely in the geometric arrangement, but in the synergistic activation of additional strengthening and toughening mechanisms. As demonstrated for harmonic-structured metals and hybrid composites, deliberately engineered structural heterogeneity enables effective load partitioning accompanied with the occurrence of pronounced plastic-strain gradients and attendant back-stress hardening. Together, these mechanisms allow such materials to avoid the long-standing strength–ductility trade-off that constrains the performance of conventional uniform nanomaterials.

sections.heading: Challenges for industrial translation
paragraphs: Despite the promising results at the laboratory scale, several critical challenges remain for the adoption of architectured metals in industry: Scale-up and continuity : Most SPD-induced architectures are still produced in batch formats and remain limited in size. Advancing toward continuous manufacturing routes, such as the cone–cone method for sheet production or continuous twist extrusion, is essential for achieving component-scale dimensions suitable for automotive, aerospace, and other industrial applications. Interface integrity : In hybrid systems produced by co-deformation, the reliability of the interface between dissimilar metals is the Achilles’ heel of the currently used processes. Future process optimization must focus on defining the processing windows (temperature, pressure, strain rate) that ensure metallurgical bonding and prevent delamination during service. Definition of quality : For conventional homogeneous materials, “quality” means uniformity. For architectured materials, we need new standards to define “controlled heterogeneity.” Quantifying the distribution of domain sizes and interface properties will be essential for quality control.

sections.heading: Future outlook: digital twins and new alloy systems
paragraphs: This article advances the idea that heterostructuring induced by severe plastic deformation offers a viable route to narrowing the gap in mechanical properties depicted schematically in Fig.  1 . Given the nascent state of this discourse, we prioritized a conceptual exposition over specific examples of mesoscale architecturing in metals, which are currently scarce. The precise boundaries of the “hole region” remain to be defined for specific materials, underscoring the need for systematic experimental investigation. We hope that this work will catalyze such research.

Moving forward, the field is likely to evolve along two strategic trajectories: Data-driven design (Digital Twins) : The complexity of 3D strain topologies in processes like twist extrusion makes trial-and-error approaches inefficient. The integration of Crystal Plasticity Finite Element Method (CPFEM) [ 45 ,  46 ] simulations with machine learning [ 47 ,  48 ] in the process design will be crucial. Developing a Digital Process Twin that predicts the final architecture and local mechanical response based on input process parameters will accelerate the design of customized architectures. Expansion to advanced alloys : While most studies have focused on simple model alloys (Cu, Al, steels), the guiding principles of deformation-enabled architecturing are applicable to more complex materials as well. Applying these strategies to high-entropy alloys (HEAs) or multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) [ 49 ,  50 ] presents a frontier opportunity. As an example, tuning the local chemical order or phase stability (e.g., TRIP/TWIP effects [ 51 ,  52 ]) for a harmonic architecture could unlock unprecedented mechanical properties, pushing the boundaries of what metallic materials can achieve.

Figure  5  outlines the roadmap for the transition to deformation-enabled architecturing of materials. To move from the current labor-intensive “trial-and-error” approach to reliable industrial continuous processing, the integration of Digital Process Twins is the way to go. As illustrated, AI-enhanced crystal plasticity (CPFEM) modeling serves as the critical bridge, enabling the virtual design and optimization of complex 3D architectures, thereby closing the gap between laboratory research and industrial application. Figure 5 Strategic roadmap for the industrial translation of deformation-enabled architecturing. The transition from  a  laboratory-scale batch processing, often reliant on trial-and-error, to  b  industrial-scale continuous manufacturing requires a paradigm shift in process design.  c  The Digital Process Twin, integrated with physics-based modeling (notably CPFEM) and data-driven AI, serves as the critical pathway. It enables the virtual prototyping of complex 3 D  strain topologies and creates a feedback loop for quality control, thereby accelerating the deployment of architectured materials in real-world engineering applications.
